To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the diabetic patients in the neuropathy group had significantly greater pressure and shear under the first metatarsal head and significantly greater shear under the fifth metatarsal head compared with the control group.
the first ray in diabetic neuropathy patients has a decreased ability to absorb and transmit forces.

(1) The longitudinal arch is supported by the first metatarsal and the plantar aponeurosis, (2) The longitudinal arch in diabetic neuropathy is not as rigid as in normal subjects and (3) In the presence of neuropathy, the plantar apneurosis can support the longitudinal arch only when the first metatarsophalangeal joint is dorsiflexed and not when it is plantar-flexed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an understanding of the biomechanical factors which contribute to the development of foot problems in neuropathic diabetics.
the design and development of a system that is capable of providing a user with the information needed to make an informed decision regarding the purchase and use of a wheelchair.
the development of an innovative and cost-effective method for measuring the pressure and shear forces under the first metatarsal head in neuropathic diabetics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the most important factors in the development of plantar pressure and foot pain are the presence of neuropathy, foot deformities and the use of ill-fitting shoes.

the evidence is not sufficient to support the use of foot orthoses to treat plantar fasciitis, and that the use of orthoses to treat other foot and ankle conditions is not supported by the evidence, with the exception of hallux limitus/rigidus and hallux valgus.
the evidence supports the notion that the diabetic neuropathic foot is a dynamic structure, and that the foot is subject to shear and pressure forces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the longitudinal arch is supported by the plantar aponeurosis and the first ray.
the longitudinal arch is not supported in the first metatarsal.
the foot is an integral part of the lower limb, which is in turn an integral part of a kinetic chain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the shear force under the first ray is greater in neuropathic patients with diabetes mellitus than in healthy subjects.
the first metatarsal head is a key structure for supporting the longitudinal arch.
we can predict the future of a patient with a diabetic foot ulcer by measuring the shear and pressure under the foot, which are the main factors that contribute to the formation of the ulcer.
